newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard meets Dalai Lama, angers China.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard meets Dalai Lama, angers China.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard met exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama on Thursday, defying threats of trade retaliation from Beijing, which urged the Australian government to "rectify" its mistake.
The Tibetan Buddhist god-king said before the meeting Howard that he would argue for "meaningful negotiations" with Beijing on the future of his Himalayan homeland.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing: "We hope the Australian government can rectify its erroneous stand and actions concerning this problem.
"The Dalai Lama is not a purely religious leader. He is a political exile who engages in splitting the motherland," Shen said.
The Dalai Lama said after his 35-minute meeting with Howard that the talks had been "very positive".
Asked if it would help the Tibetan cause, he replied: "I don't know. The Tibet issue is not easy."
But a statement from Howard's office made no mention of politics. It said the meeting had focused on religion, education and Australia's football finals this weekend.
"The two men had a relaxed discussion, largely about values and attitudes and the importance of study and learning," Howard's office said.
They discussed the importance of religious tolerance and Tibetan and Buddhist communities in Australia.

The Dalai Lama's trip to Australia was "interference in China's internal affairs...and will undoubtedly affect Sino-Australian ties, including political ties as well as trade and economic cooperation," Shen said.
"We hope Australian leaders could fully realise the gravity of this issue," he said.
China on Tuesday threatened vague trade retaliation after Howard confirmed he would meet the Dalai Lama. Beijing said the meeting would affect bilateral economic and diplomatic ties.

The Dalai Lama fled Tibet in 1959 after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule, and won the Nobel Peace Prize 30 years later for his peaceful campaign seeking autonomy for Tibet. Beijing considers him to be a separatist troublemaker.

A spokesman at China's embassy in Canberra told Australian radio that Beijing "deeply regrets" the meeting, which he said would inevitably have a negative effect on relations between China and Australia.
The spokesman said the Australian Government had allowed the Dalai Lama to visit Australia and offered him forums for anti-China activities, despite the China's objections.
Australian government leaders appeared to have no idea how seriously to take the Chinese trade threat.
Analysts said the first victims of any retaliation could be Australian banks trying to expand their links with China.
A group of 50 pro-Tibet activists waiting at Howard's office to greet the Dalai Lama praised the prime minister's decision to meet him.

Some suggested that Australia -- fresh from its diplomatic success in reviving a nuclear test ban treaty at the United Nations -- could play the role of honest broker between China and the people of Tibet.
"We were the first to begin opening the doors to China. We have the imagination. It would bring us such respect," said Melbourne campaigner Irina Surjenko.
